title: Infections in HCT and Cellular Therapy Recipients

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman was reviewed with a 3-week history of fevers and a 1-week history of painful skin nodules. She was known to have a persistent neutropenia following an allogeneic stem cell transplant 4 weeks earlier for relapsed acute lymphoblastic leukemia. She had been taking levofloxacin, voriconazole, valaciclovir, and trimethoprim– sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis; the levofloxacin had been switched to intravenous cefepime 3 weeks earlier, but her symptoms had progressed. On examination, her temperature was 103°F (39.4°C), her blood pressure was 110/68 mmHg, her heart rate was 116 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturations 98% on room air. Cardiovascular and respiratory exams were unremarkable. There were multiple subcutaneous purplish popular and nodular lesions of various sizes scattered throughout her extremities, her neck, and her chest. Some of the lesions had central necrosis. She had pedal onychomycosis. Investigations: Total white cell count 0.2 ×109 /L (4–10) Absolute neutrophil count 0.0 ×109 /L (2–8) Hemoglobin 7.4 g/dL (13–17) Platelets 43 ×109 /L (150–400) eGFR>60 mL/min/1.73 m2 Blood cultures at admission were negative, but repeat blood cultures at the point of review 3 weeks later were positive for a mold.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fusarium solani Fusarium are species of mold that may cause disseminated disease in immunocompromised patients. It tends to be more resistant to the azole antifungals than Aspergillus species but sensitive to amphotericin. Disseminated fusariosis may be identified through positive blood cultures. The typical clinical picture is as described in a patient with prolonged (>10 days) neutropenia, persistent fevers, widespread skin lesions that evolve rapidly, and blood cultures growing a mold. Unlike aspergillosis, blood cultures are commonly positive. Mortality rates are high even with appropriate antifungals and immunotherapy such as G-CSF . Because the pathogen identified is a mold, Candida tropicalis, Histoplasma capsulatum, and Cryptococcus neoformans would not be the answer, as they appear as yeast forms in the human body. However, these pathogens can cause disseminated nodular skin lesions in immunocompromised patients. Aspergillus fumigatus is not the correct answer, as voriconazole is usually effective prophylaxis against invasive aspergillus infections, and aspergillus rarely is identified in blood cultures.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q39

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with chronic myelogenous leukemia received an allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant. Her course was complicated by multiple episodes of graft-versus-host disease. She received courses of methylprednisolone. She was on maintenance immunosuppression with cyclosporine. On day 132, she developed fever and patchy pulmonary infiltrates and rapidly progressed into respiratory failure. She was intubated and underwent bronchoscopy. Branched hyphae were noted on the wet mount from the bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid. The patient was commenced on liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg daily). Four days later the laboratory reported that the BAL culture grew Scedosporium apiospermum. The patient continued having fevers, and her respiratory status was not improving.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Increase the dose of amphotericin B to 10 mg/kg daily

questions.explanation: Switch to voriconazole Scedosporium apiospermum is resistant to amphotericin B and the echinocandins. Voriconazole is the treatment of choice. Posaconazole may be used as an alternative agent. In contrast to Scedosporium apiospermum, Scedosporium prolificans (now called Lomentospora prolificans) is resistant to all antifungals. Combination treatment with amphotericin B and echinocandins or terbinafine may be of benefit due to the potential synergistic activity in L. prolificans infection.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q30

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman presented with a 5-day history of diarrhea and shortness of breath. She had experienced bloody diarrhea and associated abdominal cramps, along with a dry cough but had not had any hemoptysis, chest pain, fevers, chills, or night sweats. She had relapsed Hodgkin’s lymphoma postallogeneic stem cell transplant 2 months ago, complicated by graft versus host disease (GVHD) of the gut, skin, and lungs. She had been treated with prednisone and tacrolimus, and the GVHD was felt to be under control. She was also taking trimethoprim– sulfamethoxazole, levofloxacin, aciclovir, and voriconazole prophylaxis. She denied sick contacts and lived in an urban area. On examination, her temperature was 37.1°C, her blood pressure was 110/58 mmHg, her heart rate was 115 beats/ min, respiratory rate 24 breaths/minute, O 2 saturation 92% on 6 L/minute oxygen. She had pale conjunctivae. Respiratory examination revealed diffuse crackles bilaterally but no rhonchi or wheezes. Her abdomen was soft with mild diffuse tenderness to palpation and normal bowel sounds. There was 1+ pedal edema, and hyperpigmented areas on the arms/legs at sites of prior GVHD of the skin. Investigations: Total white cell count 3.0 ×109 /L Absolute neutrophil count 1.6 ×109 /L Hemoglobin 8 g/dL Platelets 98 ×109/L Urea, creatinine, and electrolytes were within normal limits Blood cultures: no growth at 48 hours C. difficile PCR negative Stool culture and stool ova and parasites negative CXR: bilateral interstitial infiltrates, no consolidation, no effusions CT abdomen/pelvis with and without contrast revealed diffuse colitis, no lymphadenopathy, no abscesses
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely pathogen?
questions.explanation: Cytomegalovirus Varicella may cause pneumonitis with hypoxemia in immunocompromised patients and may also cause gastrointestinal manifestations. However, the patient is on aciclovir, which is effective prophylaxis for varicella. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) causes both colitis and pneumonitis, among other manifestations. Infiltrates on imaging are usually interstitial, and diagnosis is made via CMV PCR of the blood in addition to bronchoscopy with positive transbronchial biopsy. CMV colitis may be associated with negative CMV PCR, so diagnosis would be through sigmoidoscopy with biopsy of the colon to look for CMV viral inclusions or positive immunostain on pathology. Aciclovir is not effective at preventing CMV . Strongyloides can cause both pneumonitis and gastroenteritis in immunocompromised patients, but the stool ova and parasite test is negative, and it is less common in transplant recipients who are not foreign-born or who reside in urban areas. Clostridioides difficile may cause colitis, but C. difficile PCR test is negative and has a very high sensitivity. In addition, C. difficile does not cause pneumonitis. Pneumocystis jirovecii may cause hypoxemia with interstitial pulmonary infiltrates in immunocompromised patients but does not cause colitis. In addition, this patient is on trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis, rendering pneumocystis pneumonia even less likely.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q25

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman was admitted to the hospital with a 2-day history of fever and chills, dyspnea, and left-sided pleuritic chest pain. Five months earlier she underwent hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for myelodysplastic syndrome. She was taking trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole, aciclovir, prednisone, and cyclosporine. Investigations: CXR: infiltrate in the left lower lobe
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae The patient is 5 months out from a stem cell transplant and presents with a lobar pneumonia. Although she is immunocompromised, she is on Pneumocystis prophylaxis and does not present with interstitial lung disease. CMV pneumonia would also be unlikely without a diffuse pneumonitis on imaging, and she would require histopathology with positive CMV staining to make the diagnosis. RSV pneumonia would normally present with bilateral asymmetric infiltrates and Candida spp. rarely cause pneumonia. The correct answer is therefore pneumococcal pneumonia as this patient is at risk for pneumococcal pneumonia, and a lower lobe infiltrate would fit the classic description.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q4

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman presented with a 5-day history of shortness of breath and dry cough. There was no history of fever, hemoptysis, or coryzal symptoms. She had no sick contacts and no recent travel outside of the United States. She was 60 days postallogeneic stem cell transplant for acute myelogenous leukemia. She had previously had Stevens–Johnson syndrome due to trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole. She was taking levofloxacin, valaciclovir, voriconazole, and inhaled pentamidine. On examination, her temperature was 37.2°C, blood pressure was 132/65 mmHg, heart rate 105 beats/min, respiratory rate 30 breaths/minute, oxygen saturations 88% on 2LPM of O 2. Cardiovascular exam was unremarkable; respiratory exam revealed faint bilateral crackles. There was no pedal edema, and the rest of the exam was unremarkable. Investigations: Total white cell count 1.4 ×109/L Absolute neutrophil count 0.8 ×109 /L Hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL Platelets 98 ×109 /L eGFR >60 mL/min per 1.73 m2 LDH 340 U/L Blood cultures: no growth at 48 hours CXR: diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely pathogen?
questions.explanation: Pneumocystis jirovecii Legionella and Streptococcus pneumoniae, although can cause pneumonia in transplant recipients, would be unlikely given the levofloxacin prophylaxis, which is effective treatment for both of these pathogens. Typical findings on X-ray would be consolidations. Pulmonary aspergillosis would be unusual given the patient is on voriconazole prophylaxis, and typical findings on chest X-ray tend to be cavitations with aircrescent sign or nodules rather than interstitial infiltrates. MERS coronavirus can cause hypoxemia and interstitial infiltrates on chest radiography; however, the patient has not traveled to a part of the world affected by MERS coronavirus, such as the Middle East. Although the patient is receiving inhaled pentamidine for pneumocystis prophylaxis, this is not as effective as trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole, and breakthrough infections have been reported. Thus the correct answer is Pneumocystis jirovecii.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q25

questions.question: In an allo-HSCT recipient, name 2 pathogens or groups of pathogens you would consider for prophylaxis for the pre-engraftment and post-engraftment period and an agent for each. This patient goes on to develop GVHD.

parts.text: Name 2 pathogens or groups of pathogens you would consider for prophylaxis for the pre-engraftment and post-engraftment period and an agent for each
Name one bacterial pathogen you would consider prophylaxis for (given GVHD).

cohort_answer.text: Pre-engraftment: yeast - Fluconazole; Bacteria (GNB, especially Pseudomonas) - Ciprofloxacin/levofloxacin. Post-engraftment: Pneumocystis jirovecii - Septra; CMV - Valganciclovir. GVHD: S. pneumoniae (encapsulated pathogens).

parts.text: For posaconazole prophylaxis, name three groups for which there is RCT data demonstrating decreased mortality and invasive fungal infections.

questions.model_answer: Groups with RCT evidence of reduced mortality/invasive fungal infection with posaconazole prophylaxis: (1) Patients with acute myeloid leukemia or myelodysplastic syndrome undergoing remission-induction chemotherapy with expected prolonged neutropenia. (2) Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients with graft-versus-host disease requiring intensive immunosuppression. (3) Patients with relapsed/refractory acute leukemia receiving intensive chemotherapy.
questions.beyond_mandell: Cornely et al. NEJM 2007 and Ullmann et al. NEJM 2007 posaconazole prophylaxis trials.

questions.question: A patient will be proceeding with a SCT transplant.

parts.text: What prophylaxis will you offer if HSV IgG positive?
What prophylaxis will you offer if VZV IgG positive?
What prophylaxis will you offer if Hepatitis B: HBsAg negative, HBsAb positive, HBcAb negative?
What prophylaxis will you offer if Toxoplasma IgG positive?

cohort_answer.text: HSV IgG+: Prophylaxis with (Val)Acyclovir until 1 month post transplant. VZV IgG+: Valacyclovir until day prior to VZV vaccination (no sooner than 2 years post-transplant or later if still immunosuppressed). Hepatitis B (immune pattern): Nothing. Toxoplasma IgG+: Nothing unless very high risk

questions.question: Allogenic HSCT for AML

parts.text: What are two pathogens or groups of pathogens to cover pre-transplant and two to cover post-transplant and what drugs would you use for each?
What bacterial pathogen do you need to cover post-transplant if the patient has GVHD

questions.model_answer: a) Pre-transplant (pre-engraftment, neutropenic phase): (1) HSV/VZV reactivation - acyclovir prophylaxis. (2) Invasive fungal infection (Candida/Aspergillus) - fluconazole (or posaconazole/voriconazole if mold coverage needed) prophylaxis; bacterial coverage with fluoroquinolone prophylaxis (e.g. levofloxacin) also standard during neutropenia. Post-transplant (post-engraftment, without GVHD): (1) CMV reactivation - preemptive PCR monitoring ± valganciclovir, or letermovir prophylaxis. (2) Pneumocystis jirovecii - TMP-SMX prophylaxis (started once engrafted). b) With GVHD post-transplant: encapsulated organisms (Streptococcus pneumoniae, functional asplenia-like state) - penicillin/amoxicillin or TMP-SMX prophylaxis against encapsulated bacteria given increased susceptibility from immunosuppression and impaired splenic/humoral function.
questions.beyond_mandell: Based on ASBMT/IDSA HSCT infection prevention guidelines

questions.question: CMV

parts.text: a) What are 2 strategies for post-transplant/BMT?
b) What medication would you use?

cohort_answer.text: a) Pre-emptive (monitoring); Prophylactic (give drugs). b) Ganciclovir; Valganciclovir; Letermovir. If CMV seronegative, consider valgan and letermovir prophylaxis (leukoreduced/CMV-safe blood products for transfusion).

questions.question: AM 6. AML post BMT

parts.text: a) List 2 pre-engraftment organisms/groups with the appropriate prophylaxis (2)
b. List 2 post-engraftment organisms/groups with the appropriate prophylaxis (2)
c. Name one bacteria that requires prophylaxis for post-engraftment GVHD (1)

cohort_answer.text: a) HSV - acyclovir/valacyclovir; Candida - fluconazole; Gram negative organisms - ciprofloxacin. b) Aspergillus - posaconazole; CMV - valganciclovir; PJP - septra (from engraftment >=6 weeks or until immunosuppression done). c) S. pneumoniae (in cGVHD, higher risk of encapsulated organisms; prophylax with PCN, TMP/SMX, or Levo).

questions.question: Post HSCT.

parts.text: Name 2 organisms and prophylaxis in pre engraftment and post engraftment.
Name 1 organism to worry about post-engraftment if he develops GVHD.

questions.model_answer: a) Pre-engraftment: HSV/VZV - acyclovir prophylaxis; invasive fungal infection (Candida/Aspergillus) - fluconazole or mold-active azole prophylaxis. Post-engraftment (no GVHD): CMV - preemptive PCR-guided therapy or letermovir prophylaxis; Pneumocystis jirovecii - TMP-SMX prophylaxis. b) Post-engraftment with GVHD: encapsulated bacteria (Streptococcus pneumoniae) given functional hyposplenism/impaired humoral immunity - penicillin prophylaxis.

parts.text: Name 2 pathogens or group of pathogens and an appropriate prophylaxis regimen for each, in table format (Pathogen | Regimen) for the Pre-engraftment and Post-engraftment periods

questions.model_answer: Pre-engraftment: HSV/VZV - acyclovir; Invasive fungal infection (Candida/Aspergillus) - fluconazole (or posaconazole/voriconazole if high mold risk). Post-engraftment: CMV - preemptive PCR-guided valganciclovir or letermovir prophylaxis; Pneumocystis jirovecii - TMP-SMX prophylaxis.

questions.question: Allo HSCT for AML.

parts.text: Table: 2 pathogens and associated ppx for pre engraftment and 2 pathogens post-engraftment.
What bacterial pathogen ppx if GVHD during engraftment.

questions.model_answer: a) Pre-engraftment: (1) HSV/VZV - acyclovir prophylaxis. (2) Invasive fungal infection (Candida/Aspergillus) - fluconazole or mold-active azole prophylaxis. Post-engraftment: (1) CMV - preemptive PCR monitoring/letermovir prophylaxis. (2) Pneumocystis jirovecii - TMP-SMX prophylaxis. b) Bacterial prophylaxis if GVHD during engraftment: penicillin (or TMP-SMX) against encapsulated organisms (Streptococcus pneumoniae) given functional asplenia/impaired humoral immunity from GVHD and its treatment.

questions.question: Post BMT with hemorrhagic cystitis

parts.text: What is the most likely cause if this occurred 5 days from transplant
Name 3 causes if this occurred 5 weeks from transplant

cohort_answer.text: 5 days: Early hemorrhagic cystitis (esp 24-72hr out, up to 2wk) is most commonly from drug toxicities (e.g. alkylating agents like cyclophosphamide, radiation therapy). 5 weeks: Adenovirus; BK, JC virus; CMV

questions.question: Patient about to undergo bone marrow transplant. For each scenario, describe what you would like to do in terms of intervention.

parts.text: HSV IgG positive
VZV IgG positive
Hepatitis B HBsAg negative, HBsAb positive, HBcAb negative
Toxoplasma IgG positive

cohort_answer.text: HSV IgG positive: Acyclovir prophylaxis for at least 1 year post transplant (some institutions until immune restoration 2 years with no ongoing IS or cGVHD); AHS guide: valacyclovir accepted until 1-month post-transplant, controversial until 3 months (possibly useful for HSV seropositive recipients with HSV seronegative donors); irrelevant for patients on VZV prophylaxis, who get valacyclovir anyway. VZV IgG positive: Acyclovir prophylaxis at least 1 year post transplant; use valacyclovir followed by VZV vaccination (effective for eliminating post-herpetic neuralgia); give valacyclovir until VZV vaccination at 24 months post-transplant in patients free of active cGVHD and off immunosuppressive therapy, or >=3 months after discontinuation of immunosuppressive therapy when cGVHD inactive. Hepatitis B (HBsAg neg, HBsAb pos, HBcAb neg): Nothing - patient was previously immune and has no evidence of infection. Toxoplasma IgG positive: Generally no specific prophylaxis for toxo in HSCT but patient would be receiving PJP prophylaxis for at least 6 months post-transplant

questions.question: You see a patient who underwent hematopoietic stem cell transplant 1 month ago. He is found to have a positive CMV PCR.

parts.text: List FIVE risk factors for CMV infection in hematopoietic stem cell transplant.
Describe prophylactic therapy and pre-emptive therapy.
How is ganciclovir cleared and in what population is dose adjustment required?
List THREE alternate medications that can be used with mutations in UL97 and ONE alternate medication that can be used with mutations in UL54.

questions.model_answer: a) Five risk factors for CMV in HSCT: (1) CMV-seropositive recipient (D+/R+ or D-/R+ - recipient seropositivity is main driver of reactivation). (2) Donor/recipient CMV serostatus mismatch (D+/R-). (3) Type of transplant - allogeneic (especially mismatched/unrelated donor or cord blood) higher risk than autologous. (4) Graft-versus-host disease and its immunosuppressive treatment. (5) T-cell depletion (in vivo, e.g. ATG/alemtuzumab, or ex vivo graft manipulation). b) Prophylactic therapy: antiviral (letermovir preferred in HSCT, or valganciclovir) given to all at-risk patients from early post-transplant through a defined high-risk period regardless of PCR status. Pre-emptive therapy: serial quantitative CMV PCR monitoring, initiating treatment (valganciclovir/ganciclovir) only once viremia is detected above a defined threshold, before end-organ disease develops. c) Ganciclovir clearance: renally cleared, excreted largely unchanged in urine; dose adjustment required in renal impairment (reduced eGFR). d) UL97 mutation alternatives (3): foscarnet, cidofovir, maribavir. UL54 mutation alternative (1): foscarnet (cidofovir may retain some activity depending on specific mutation, but foscarnet is the standard alternative).

questions.question: Q56 2023 Part 2. Invasive aspergillosis in a BMT patient. (FUNGAL)

parts.text: 3 radiographic findings consistent with IPA
Preferred treatment
AKI and prolonged QTc, what is best treatment option

cohort_answer.text:
3 radiographic findings (Mandell IPA CT findings): diffuse nodular infiltrates; halo sign (density surrounded by a ring of low-attenuation, early sign); classic pleural-based wedge density (early, less common); cavity lesions (late); pleural effusions; 'crescent sign' (nodular lesion that cavitates).
Preferred treatment (IDSA Aspergillus Guidelines): Voriconazole. Alternates: ampho B liposomal, isavuconazole, or other lipid formulations of ampho B. Echinocandin monotherapy not recommended.
Best option with AKI/QTc prolongation: For AKI - Voriconazole (oral) or isavuconazole do not require dose adjustment; IV voriconazole contains cyclodextrin which theoretically accumulates renally, but not clinically demonstrated; IDSA states relative benefits/risks of IV voriconazole in renal failure should be individualized. For QTc prolongation: Isavuconazole, which 'shortens the QTc, clinical significance unclear'.

questions.question: Q10 (2004 PM). Post-BMT with respiratory symptoms

parts.text: A) List the organisms possibly involved
B) Treatment
C) Further investigations

cohort_answer.text: A) Invasive aspergillosis, mucormycosis; CAP including atypicals; viral pneumonia including CMV pneumonitis; PJP; Nocardia; NTM, TB; disseminated Strongyloides. Non-infectious: GVHD, PTLD, cryptogenic organizing pneumonia. B) Depends if also neutropenic; empiric Ceftriaxone + Azithro for CAP; +/- Septra and steroids for PJP if not already on ppx and acutely unwell; +/- voriconazole for aspergillus if not already on ppx. C) Respiratory viral PCR on NP aspirate; CT chest; bronchoscopy with BAL (tissue to histopathology); CMV tissue to assess invasive disease; PJP and legionella PCR, AFB/fungal/bacterial culture; +/- lung biopsy if peripheral nodule (also for PTLD).

questions.question: A patient is 30 days out from an allogeneic transplant which was complicated by severe candida mucositis and treated with fluconazole. Now has increasing LFTs.

parts.text: What is the probable cause?
What would you do with this patient now? Justify your answer

cohort_answer.text: A) Fluconazole-induced hepatotoxicity. DDX: hepatosplenic candidiasis (manifests at engraftment, median presentation 2-3 weeks post-HSCT if no ppx); CMV/VZV/EBV/HHV6/HSV/HBV (HSV highest risk pre-engraftment, usually on ppx); hepatic sinusoidal obstruction syndrome/VOD (elevated bili, hepatomegaly/RUQ pain, sudden weight gain, needs biopsy; risk factors liver dysfunction pre-tx, poorly matched donor, MTX for GVHD ppx); acute GVHD; other drugs (calcineurin inhibitor, methotrexate, TMP-SMX). B) CT abdomen/pelvis to work up hepatosplenic candidiasis; blood cultures for yeast; once cultures obtained, stop fluconazole, start echinocandin; if azole required use Posaconazole (reduced transaminitis); IDSA alternative: IV echinocandin or IV lipid formulation AmB 3-5mg/kg daily; start empiric acyclovir for HSV if not on ppx; trend liver enzymes; look for non-infectious causes; consider esophageal brushings for yeast culture/sensitivity, Herpesviridae viral load.

questions.question: Name 2 pathogens or groups of pathogens and an appropriate prophylaxis regimen for each: Bacteria (mainly gram negative including Pseudomonas); Fungus; Herpesviridae

parts.text: Bacteria
Fungus
Herpesviridae

cohort_answer.text: Bacteria: FQ ppx for high-risk patients with prolonged/profound neutropenia - Levofloxacin 500mg daily or ciprofloxacin 500mg BID, until end of neutropenia/engraftment or last chemo dose; prolonged ppx (>100d post-HSCT) only for S. pneumo prevention in allogeneic recipients with chronic GVHD on chemo. Fungus: Candida ppx for all HSCT or intensive remission-induction/salvage chemo for acute leukemia - Fluconazole 400mg daily (until engraftment or 75 days post-transplant, or until immunosuppression discontinued for secondary ppx); mold ppx (Aspergillus, Mucor) for highest-risk HSCT post-engraftment with GVHD - Voriconazole (no mucor coverage) or Posaconazole (covers mucor, liquid 200mg TID or delayed release 300mg BID day1 then 300mg daily); PJP ppx - TMP/SMX 1 DS tab daily, 1 SS tab daily, or 1 DS tab 3x/week. Herpesviridae: HSV ppx with acyclovir 800mg BID in all HSV+ HSCT/acute leukemia induction patients, until engraftment/resolution of mucositis (~30d), extended to 1 year for secondary ppx; CMV ppx for CMV r+ or r-/d+ with CMV safe blood products, Ganciclovir/Valganciclovir for 100d post-HSCT or Letermovir; VZV ppx for VZV r+ with Acyclovir or Valacyclovir 500mg BID for 1 year post-HSCT.

questions.question: Q11 (2007). Woman 3 weeks post-BMT, known CMV+, HSV+. Acute respiratory illness with bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. BAL = 3+ HSV. Name 3 possible causes other than HSV

parts.text: Name 3 possible causes other than HSV

cohort_answer.text: Infectious: bacterial pneumonia, viral pneumonia (influenza, COVID, RSV, parainfluenza), adenovirus, aspergillus, CMV pneumonitis (less likely given timeline). Non-infectious: pulmonary edema, alveolar hemorrhage, ARDS, GVHD, idiopathic pneumonia, organizing pneumonia.

questions.question: Man who is pre-HSCT, HSV serology is positive.

parts.text: When would you start ppx?
Duration?
What would you use?
Is it important to know the HSV status of the donor?
Why/why not (donor HSV status)?

cohort_answer.text: A) Start of conditioning. B) Ppx until WBC recovery AND mucositis resolution; can be extended to a year if frequent recurrent HSV infections, GVHD, or needs ongoing VZV ppx. C) Acyclovir 400mg PO BID in adults; Valacyclovir 500mg PO daily. D) No. E) HSV is only latent in dorsal root/sensory ganglia.

questions.question: Post BMT patient at 15 months. Exposed to room-mate with chicken pox.

parts.text: What do you do? Period of infectivity for the patient?
What are the vaccines indicated for her at 12 months assuming well and no immune suppression
When can you give VZV vaccine for her and what would be 2 contraindications at that time?

cohort_answer.text: A) Confirm diagnosis; incubation 14-16 days (range 10-21); infectivity 24-48h pre-exanthem until all lesions crusted (day 8-21 post-exposure isolation, 28 if VZIG used); confirm vaccine/infection/serologic status; VZV-seronegative HCT recipients transplanted within previous 24 months (or >24 months if continued immunosuppression e.g. chronic GVHD) should get VariZIG within 10 days of contact; seropositive but highly immunosuppressed patients should also get VariZIG; cannot give vaccine post-BMT until at least 2 years; isolate roommate in airborne; isolate BMT patient in airborne from day 8 post-exposure until day 28 (VZIG given). B) Immunize with 2 doses of Shingrix at least 1 year after herpes zoster episode; other vaccines 12 months post-BMT include 3 doses PCV at 3-6 months then PPV-23 at 12-18 months, HiB conjugate 3 doses at 6 months, Td at 6 months, inactivated polio at 6 months, HepB 3 doses at 6 months, HPV 3 doses at 6 months, meningococcal at 6 months, influenza 4-6 months post-transplant; live vaccines (MMR, varicella, YF) at 24 months post-BMT. C) Live attenuated Zostavax: wait 24 months post-transplant; inactivated Shingrix: wait 3-6 months post-transplant. Contraindications: hypersensitivity reaction; ongoing immunosuppression (for GVHD); IVIG (last 8-11 months).

questions.question: RSV in a BMT patient.

parts.text: Management?

cohort_answer.text: Oral Ribavirin 15-20mg/kg/day divided TID x10 days; toxicities include teratogenicity (long t1/2), hemolytic anemia, leukopenia, cough/dyspnea/bronchoconstriction, neuropsychologic symptoms; can also consider IVIG and palivizumab.

questions.question: List 4 vaccines contraindicated in the first year post-BMT

parts.text: List 4 vaccines contraindicated in the first year post-BMT

cohort_answer.text: Any 4 live vaccines: MMR, Varicella vaccine, live HZ vaccine (Zostavax), Rotavirus, Yellow fever, live Japanese encephalitis vaccine, BCG, live influenza vaccine.

questions.question: In a patient 2 years post-transplant (it is November)

parts.text: A reason not to vaccinate?
2 vaccines that are a priority for household members?

cohort_answer.text: A) If patient still immunosuppressed + GVHD, may not respond to vaccines and live attenuated vaccines contraindicated; current/recent IVIG administration (lack of vaccine efficacy) in the last 8-11 months. B) Household members should prioritize transmissible vaccine-preventable diseases: flu, Hep A/B, Pneumococcus, Pertussis, HiB, Rotavirus, MMRV, Zoster (also note MMRV vaccine viruses not transmitted to contacts; zoster and vaccinia rare shedding; rotavirus sheds in stool up to 4 weeks).

questions.question: Describe your approach to vaccination over the first 2 years post-BMT?

parts.text: Approach to vaccination over first 2 years post-BMT

cohort_answer.text: Pre-HSCT: if time permits, give all routine inactivated vaccines appropriate for age, conjugate pneumococcal vaccine regardless of age (ideally Pneu-C-20), polysaccharide pneumococcal if age ≥2 + Pneu-C-13/15, inactivated influenza if flu season; give inactivated vaccines ≥2 weeks before transplant; live vaccines not within 4 weeks of conditioning start. Post-HSCT: treat allogeneic same as autologous; consider all as never immunized and re-immunize (bone marrow ablation eliminates immune memory); poor response to polysaccharide vaccines; measure post-vaccination titres if possible; higher risk for pneumococcus, Hib, measles, varicella, influenza. Schedule: DTP 3 doses from 6-12 months post-HSCT; Hib 3 doses from 6-12 months; HepB 3-4 doses at 6-12 months (double dose); HPV 3 doses at 6-12 months; influenza (inactivated) annually from 4-6 months; quadrivalent meningococcal conjugate 2 doses from 6 months (if asplenic); PNEU-C-20 primary series 3 doses starting 3-9 months (≥4 weeks apart) + booster at 12-18 months; inactivated polio 3 doses at 6-12 months. Live vaccines (MMR, varicella) at 24 months post-BMT if no GVHD, immunosuppression stopped >3 months, disease inactive, and immunocompetent; YF vaccine possible if criteria met and travelling to endemic area; IVIG inactivates live vaccines so delay 8-11 months after last IVIG dose.

questions.question: Q9 (2009 AM). Immunocompromised - post BMT - pneumonitis. Four viruses of different families that could also cause this

parts.text: Name four viruses of different families that could cause pneumonitis in this setting

cohort_answer.text: Cytomegalovirus (Herpesviridae); Enterovirus (Picornaviridae); Adenovirus (Adenoviridae); Parainfluenza (Paramyxoviridae); Influenza (Orthomyxoviridae).

questions.question:
Q68 (2018)
A patient will be proceeding with a SCT transplant. What prophylaxis will you offer in each of these independent scenarios?

parts.text: A) HSV IgG positive:
B) VZV IgG +
C) Hep B sAg neg, sAb +, cAb neg

cohort_answer.text:
A: Valacyclovir 500mg PO daily 30 days post transplant (preferred). Acyclovir 400 PO bid 30 days post transplant. Some recommend continuing for 3-6 months after transplant. Dosing for Lung transplant (Vala 500mg bid, Acyclovir 400mg q6h)

B: Acyclovir 200mg 3-5x/day x 3-6 months after transplant

C: Immune, no ppx needed

questions.question: Post HSCT and develops CMV DNAemia.

parts.text: What are 5 risk factors for CMV disease
Define pre-emptive and prophylaxis strategies (no advantages/disadvantages, just describe)
How is IV ganciclovir metabolized, and when might the dose need adjusting
For resistant CMV disease, name three antivirals that may be considered for UL97 mutation and one for UL54 mutation.

cohort_answer.text: Risk factors: CMV seropositivity (D-/R+); T cell depletion (ATG); GVHD; Immunosuppressive drugs (steroids, alemtuzumab); Lymphopenia. Pre-emptive therapy: Patients monitored frequently (weekly) with CMV load and antiviral therapy initiated when viral replication reaches a certain assay threshold defined at each institution. Prophylaxis: Immediate start of prophylaxis (ganciclovir, valganciclovir, letermovir) post-transplant in high risk patients. Ganciclovir metabolism: Acyclic analog of nucleoside guanosine, converted intracellularly to ganciclovir 5'-monophosphate by viral kinase encoded by CMV gene UL97 during infection; cellular kinases catalyze formation of ganciclovir diphosphate and triphosphate (10-fold greater concentration in CMV infected cells); ganciclovir triphosphate is a competitive inhibitor of dGTP incorporation into DNA, preferentially inhibiting viral DNA polymerases, and is a poor substrate for chain elongation, disrupting viral DNA synthesis. Dose adjustment needed: Renal impairment; Dialysis; Pre-emptive therapy (induction 5mg/kg q12 vs maintenance 5mg/kg q24); UL97 mutation for <5x (10mg/kg q12, off-label); Intravitreal injection (off-label). Resistant CMV: UL97 mutation - Foscarnet, Cidofovir, Maribavir, possibly high dose ganciclovir. UL54 mutation - Maribavir, Foscarnet (avoid cidofovir)

questions.question: 26. In patients with high risk neutropenia, describe two advantages and two disadvantages of preemptive prophylaxis over empiric prophylaxis for invasive fungal infection.

parts.text: Describe two advantages and two disadvantages of preemptive prophylaxis over empiric prophylaxis for invasive fungal infection.

cohort_answer.text: Pre-emptive often involves serial HRCT and Galactomannan/B-D-Glucan. Advantages: Decreased costs of antifungal drugs; lower risk of resistance; minimises risk of drug related toxicity. Disadvantages: Requires frequent testing; delayed start of therapy; higher rates of invasive fungal infection.

questions.question: Causes of hemorrhagic cystitis 5 days post allo cell transplant

parts.text: Causes of hemorrhagic cystitis 5 days post allo cell transplant
4 causes if it happened 5 months post tx

questions.model_answer: a) Causes of hemorrhagic cystitis at 5 days post allo-HSCT (early, pre-engraftment): chemotherapy/conditioning toxicity - cyclophosphamide (acrolein metabolite) or busulfan-based conditioning regimen toxicity; radiation cystitis from total body irradiation. b) Four causes if occurring at 5 months post-transplant (late, viral): (1) BK virus (most common late cause). (2) Adenovirus. (3) CMV. (4) JC virus (less common) - also consider GVHD-related or drug-induced causes.

questions.question: 14 year old female who underwent allogeneic stem cell transplant 21 days ago for relapsed AML. She is experiencing dysuria and hematuria. You suspect BK virus hemorrhagic cystitis.

parts.text: What are 4 risk factors for BK virus hemorrhagic cystitis in allogeneic stem cell transplant?
What urine based test other than blood can be used for diagnosis?
What are 2 antivirals from different classes that can be used for treatment?

questions.model_answer:
a) Four risk factors for BK hemorrhagic cystitis after allogeneic HSCT: (1) myeloablative conditioning regimen (2) acute graft-versus-host disease (3) BKV seropositivity/high anti-BKV IgG before transplant (4) greater degree of immunosuppression/lymphopenia (also unrelated or HLA-mismatched donor).
b) Urine-based test: urine cytology for decoy cells, or quantitative BK viral PCR (viruria) - BK viral load in urine typically exceeds that in blood in cystitis.
c) Two antivirals from different classes: (1) Cidofovir (nucleotide analog DNA polymerase inhibitor) (2) A fluoroquinolone such as levofloxacin (inhibits BKV-encoded DNA gyrase/topoisomerase); leflunomide (immunomodulatory DHODH inhibitor) is another accepted alternative-class option.

questions.question: Q72 2023 Day 1. AutoSCT with BK hemorrhagic cystitis. (VIRUSES)

parts.text: 4 risk factors
One urinary test to diagnose, in addition to her symptoms
Which 2 antiviral drugs to treat

cohort_answer.text:
4 risk factors: Myeloablative conditioning regimens (HLA mismatch higher risk); haploidentical donor; GVHD (acute and chronic); CMV reactivation; male sex.
Urinary test/symptoms: Typically BK viruria; BKPyV serum can help with diagnosis; BK viremia >10,000 copies/mL more likely to occur; symptoms - cystitis (dysuria, urgency, abdominal pain), hematuria, AKI.
2 antiviral drugs: Intravesicular and IV Cidofovir (no RCT data, some observational studies); Brincidofovir (pro-drug of Cidofovir); Leflunomide (has some antiviral properties against BKV).

questions.question: Vaccines in HSCT/SOT transplant patients

parts.text: When is the earliest you can give inactivated vaccines pre-transplant?
When is the earliest you can give inactivated vaccines post-transplant?

cohort_answer.text: A) Inactivated vaccines: at least 2 weeks before conditioning. Live attenuated vaccines: at least 4 weeks before conditioning. B) SOT: live vaccines not recommended post-SOT; inactivated vaccine wait 3-6 months post-transplant or when maintenance immunosuppression attained; HepB at double usual dose; HPV 3-dose schedule regardless of age. HSCT: live vaccine around 24 months post-transplant if immunocompetent and no GVHD; inactivated vaccine 6-12 months post-transplant; COVID (3 doses + boosters) can begin 3-6 months post-transplant.
